passage: Every morning that month, Vinita reached the bus stop later than her friends. She had ironed her kurta twice with the heavy coal iron and tried her hair in three different partings. Since her cousin's phone had shown her the town girls' pictures, all smooth skin and glowing eyes, her own face in the steel mirror seemed wrong somehow. At Rafiq's tea stall she stood behind the sacks, checking her reflection in a glass jar. Rafiq, who had known her since she was small, set down a cup. "Beti, those pictures are polished by a machine before anyone sees them. Dress how it pleases you. That's your choice, it isn't what you're worth." She smiled, not fully believing him. "If it keeps sitting heavy on you," he added, "tell your mother or your teacher."

qa.q: How many times did Vinita iron her kurta?
qa.a: She ironed her kurta twice with the heavy coal iron.

qa.q: How might Vinita be feeling about her own face, and what shows it?
qa.a: She feels unsure or dissatisfied, shown by the repeated ironing, the changed partings and the checking of her reflection; her half-believing smile suggests she is only partly reassured.

qa.q: What would help Vinita if the worry does not ease?
qa.a: Talking to a trusted adult such as her mother or her teacher, as Rafiq suggested, so that lasting distress gets caring attention.

qa.q: Why might Rafiq's words carry weight with Vinita?
qa.a: He has known her since she was small, so the comment comes from a familiar, caring adult and not from someone judging her looks.

grounding: A teen compares herself with filtered pictures and over-controls grooming; a supportive adult says presentation is a choice, not worth.

passage: The bus horn sounded outside the Manchester terrace, and Chidi was still pulling on his fourth shirt. Paulo waited on the step, hood up against the drizzle. "You looked fine three shirts ago." "You haven't seen what the older boys post," Chidi said, tugging at the collar. "Their arms, their skin, everything perfect." "They pick one out of forty and put it through a filter. My cousin does it." Paulo shrugged. "My mum says clothes are a choice, not a scoreboard." Chidi gave a short, stiff laugh and put the first shirt back on. On the bus Paulo sent a message: talk to me if it gets heavy, or to your form tutor.

qa.q: How many shirts had Chidi tried on when the horn sounded?
qa.a: He was pulling on his fourth shirt.

qa.q: What might Chidi be worried about when he compares himself with the older boys?
qa.a: He may be afraid that his own looks don't measure up to their perfect pictures; his stiff laugh suggests the comparison is bothering him more than he admits.

qa.q: What small step could help Chidi if the comparing continues?
qa.a: He could talk to Paulo or his form tutor, as Paulo suggested, and remember that the photos were picked and filtered.

qa.q: How might Paulo feel watching his friend change shirts again and again?
qa.a: He is probably concerned but trying to stay light, which is why he jokes first and then sends a quiet message offering to listen.

grounding: A teen over-controls clothes after comparing with filtered images, and a friend frames presentation as choice and offers support.

passage:
In the boys' school in Pune, Tushar had started arriving late. Ishita Ma'am, his class teacher, noticed his hair was always perfectly set, and he'd sometimes leave class to check it in the washroom mirror.
On Wednesday he arrived at the second period, red-eyed. At lunch she asked him to help carry books to the staff room.
"You've been late a lot. Is everything okay?"
He stared at the floor. "My hair wouldn't go right. I look horrible compared to everyone online. I couldn't come like that."
Ishita Ma'am didn't laugh. "How you style yourself is your choice, and it's fine to care. But it doesn't decide what you're worth. You're the best debater in 9B."
He gave a small smile.
She didn't stop there. That evening she phoned his parents to share what she'd noticed, and they agreed to keep an eye on it together and to talk to the counsellor if it went on.

qa.q: Where did Tushar go to check his hair?
qa.a: He'd leave class to check it in the washroom mirror.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he explained why he was late?
qa.a: Tushar felt distressed and ashamed, comparing himself to people online and feeling he looked horrible.

qa.q: Which of Ishita Ma'am's actions were most helpful?
qa.a: She listened without laughing, said presentation is a choice but not a measure of worth, and, because the distress was lasting, informed his parents and planned a counsellor chat if it continued.

qa.q: How might Tushar's classmates have seen his lateness?
qa.a: They may have thought he was just careless or vain, without knowing he was struggling with how he looked.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager over-controlling his grooming after comparing with filtered images, and a teacher stressing value over looks while watching for lasting distress.

passage:
Indu didi,
You said to write when things feel heavy. So.
Lately I change my shirt five or six times before leaving the house. Every photo on my feed is some guy with perfect skin and a jawline, and filters make even my friends look like that. Then I look in the mirror and just see my nose.
Yesterday I didn't go to Farzan's birthday because none of my shirts looked right. I sat in my room instead.
I know it sounds silly. Ammi says I'm handsome, but she has to say that.
You told me once that you used to hate your curly hair, and now you love it. How did that happen?
Please don't tell anyone I wrote this. Well, maybe Ammi, if you think it's important. I'm tired of feeling like this.
Farhan

qa.q: How many times does Farhan change his shirt before leaving?
qa.a: Farhan changes his shirt five or six times.

qa.q: What is Farhan feeling in the letter?
qa.a: Farhan feels insecure and tired of the constant comparison, ashamed of his looks, and a little hopeful that Indu can help.

qa.q: How could Indu best support Farhan?
qa.a: Indu could reply warmly, remind Farhan that clothes and looks are choices, not a measure of worth, and since the distress is lasting and events are being missed, gently involve Ammi as Farhan half-suggests.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel if she knew about the missed birthday?
qa.a: She would probably feel worried and sad, and want to help rather than just repeating that Farhan is handsome.

grounding: The letter shows a teenager comparing looks with filtered images and over-controlling clothes, with the chance for supportive adults to respond.

passage:
So, Sahil, you asked about filters on this show. I'm Ojas, and last year I couldn't post a single photo without editing my face. Smoother skin, sharper chin, even my eyes bigger.
Then it went further. I wouldn't go out if my hair was wrong. I stopped playing football because I sweated and looked "bad." I checked mirrors everywhere.
My mother noticed. Not the first day. But after a few weeks of me skipping things, she sat with me one night and said, "You seem really unhappy. Is it about how you look?"
I cried, honestly. She didn't say "don't be silly." She said, "You can dress how you want. But you are not your face." And the next week she came with me to the school counsellor.
It got better slowly. I still like nice hair. I just don't cancel my life for it.

qa.q: What did Ojas stop playing?
qa.a: Ojas stopped playing football.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling during that year?
qa.a: Ojas felt unhappy and anxious about appearance, comparing constantly and avoiding things out of shame.

qa.q: Which of the mother's responses helped most?
qa.a: Noticing the lasting change, asking gently, saying clothes were a free choice but Ojas was not a face, and going along to the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Ojas's football teammates have seen him quitting?
qa.a: They might have thought Ojas had lost interest, without knowing it was about body image and fear of looking bad.

grounding: The spoken account shows a teenager over-controlling appearance after comparing to filtered images and a parent responding to lasting distress.

passage: I'm Lavanya, and I share a room with Indu-didi, so I notice things. Since the summer she has been taking twenty selfies before school and deleting nineteen. She runs the filter that makes skin look like glass, then frowns at her real face in the mirror, as if the mirror got it wrong. On Monday she changed her kurta three times and missed the bus. On Wednesday she said she looked "disgusting" in the class photo. I thought she looked like Indu. I don't know what goes on in her head; I only see the outside. That evening I told Amma about the deleted selfies. Amma didn't lecture. She sat on Didi's bed and said, "Wear what you like, change your hair, all of it is your choice. None of it is what you're worth." Didi rolled her eyes, but she didn't leave the room. Amma kept checking in, and on Friday she took Didi for a walk, just the two of them.

qa.q: How many selfies does Indu take before school?
qa.a: Indu takes twenty selfies before school and deletes nineteen.

qa.q: What might Indu be feeling when she frowns at the mirror?
qa.a: Indu seems unhappy and self-conscious, comparing her real face with the glassy filtered one; since Lavanya only sees the outside, it might also be ordinary morning stress.

qa.q: How did Amma support Indu?
qa.a: Amma didn't lecture, told Indu that clothes and hair are her choice but not her worth, and kept checking in, taking her for a walk on Friday.

qa.q: How does Lavanya see Indu in the class photo?
qa.a: To Lavanya, Indu just looked like Indu, not 'disgusting', which shows how differently Indu was seeing herself.

grounding: It shows a teenager comparing herself with filtered images and over-controlling clothes, and a parent stressing presentation as a choice, not a measure of worth, while watching over time.
